import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 189

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/189](https://www.erdosproblems.com/189)
-/

open Affine EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos189

/-- Erdős problem 189 asked whether the below holds for all rectangles. -/
def Erdos189For (P : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → Prop) (A : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ) :=
    ∀ᵉ (n > 0) (colouring : ℝ² → Fin n), ∃ colour, ∀ area > (0 : ℝ), ∃ a b c d,
      {a, b, c, d} ⊆ colouring⁻¹' {colour} ∧
      IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a, b, c, d] ∧
      A a b c d = area ∧
      P a b c d

/--
If $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finitely coloured then must there exist some colour class which contains the
vertices of a rectangle of every area?

Graham, "On Partitions of 𝔼ⁿ", Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 28, 89-91 (1980).
(See "Concluding Remarks" on page 96.)

Solved (with answer `False`, as formalised below) in:
Vjekoslav Kovač, "Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume", 2023
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09973
In fact, Kovač's colouring is even Jordan measurable (the topological boundary of each
monochromatic region is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero).

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev and Kovac using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos189.lean"]
theorem erdos_189 :
    answer(False) ↔ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/-- Graham claims this is "easy to see". -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.square :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction ∧
        dist a b = dist b c)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/--
Seems to be open, as of January 2025.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.parallelogram :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b] ∥ line[ℝ, c, d] ∧
        line[ℝ, a, d] ∥ line[ℝ, b, c])
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin) := by
  sorry

end Erdos189

findings.description: The declaration asserts `¬ Erdos189For ...`, choosing a negative conjectural answer to the parallelogram problem. The cited sources instead pose the yes-or-no question without choosing that answer. This could be an intentional negative conjecture, but that polarity choice is not supported by the references and excludes a positive answer without changing the statement. This is a modelling concern, not a stale-status issue: `research open` agrees with the sources.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/189 says that the same question can be asked for parallelograms and that it remains open. Kovač, arXiv:2309.09973v3, §1.3, explicitly asks: “If R² is finitely colored then must there exist some color-class which contains the vertices of a parallelogram of every given area?” He discusses the possibility of a positive answer; he does not state the negative as a conjecture.
findings.suggested_fix: Represent the source question as `answer(sorry) ↔ Erdos189For ...`, retaining the existing parallelogram predicate, area function, and `research open` category. Alternatively, document and cite an explicitly intended negative conjecture.

findings.description: The docstring gives Graham’s article page range as 89–91. The correct range is 89–97; the separately cited concluding remarks on page 96 are correctly located.
findings.source_evidence: The bibliography at https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/189, Graham’s publication list at https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/, and Crossref DOI 10.1016/0097-3165(80)90061-8 all give 89–97. The article itself continues through page 97.

reformulations.difference: The area formula uses the sine of the oriented angle `∡ a b c`, without an absolute value, rather than the usual unsigned interior-angle formula.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a,b,c,d]` requires `(∡ a b c).sign = 1`. In Mathlib this sign is the sign of the sine, and `oangle_eq_angle_of_sign_eq_one` identifies this oriented angle with the unsigned angle. Consequently the formula is exactly `dist a b * dist b c * Real.sin (∠ a b c)`. Every nondegenerate parallelogram can be cyclically labelled in the required orientation. The scratch theorem `Review189.area_formula_reformulation` proves the full `Erdos189For` equivalence between these two area functions, for arbitrary shape predicate P.

reformulations.difference: Rectangles are specified using a strictly convex ordered quadrilateral and only three consecutive perpendicularity conditions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The polygon condition excludes repeated vertices and collinear triples. The three conditions therefore give genuine right interior angles at b, c, and d. The interior angles of a convex quadrilateral sum to 2π, forcing the fourth angle to be π/2, so this is precisely a rectangle. Conversely, any nondegenerate rectangle can be labelled in the required cyclic orientation and satisfies the three conditions. The adjacent-side product is its usual area.

review.notes: All four declarations were reviewed. The rectangle’s negative answer, the solved square variant, and the open status of the parallelogram question agree with the sources. Scratch files `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` and `/workspace/review/boundary.lean` compile successfully. Without using the problem theorems, they prove pairwise distinctness of the four vertices, positivity and equivalence of the area formula, and explicit witnesses satisfying all three shape predicates for every positive area in any one-colouring. Their printed axioms contain no `sorryAx`. The external proof’s final statement matches the rectangle claim up to symmetry of ↔; its relevant definitions and proof dependencies were inspected, with no sorry or custom axioms found. Its original Lean 4.24.0 project was not rebuilt in this Lean 4.33.1 sandbox. No repository files were edited.
